items.title: Section: What Should Be Looked At — Old Age, Illness, and Death

items.zh: 何色類色是所應觀？謂諸所有衰老朽邁上氣者身、傴僂憑杖戰掉者身。或諸疾苦重病者身，腳腫、手腫、腹腫、面腫、膚色萎黃、瘡癬、疥癩、眾苦逼迫、身形委頓、身形洪爛、諸根闇鈍。或有夭喪，死經一日、或經二日、或經七日，被諸烏鵲、餓狗、鵄鷲、狐狼、野干種種暴惡傍生禽獸之所食噉。或命終已，出置高床，上施幰帳，前後大眾或哀或哭，以其灰土塵坌身髮，生愁、生苦、生悲、生怨、生憂、生惱。如是等類所有眾色，我應觀察。觀是眾色，能順梵行、能攝梵行、能令諸善尋思現行。
items.en: What class of forms should be observed? The bodies of those aged and worn down, gasping for breath, bent double, leaning on a staff, trembling as they move. Or the bodies of those gravely ill — feet swollen, hands swollen, abdomen swollen, face swollen, skin sallow and withered, covered in sores, scabies, or leprous lesions, oppressed by manifold suffering, the body wasted, or the body's flesh decayed and rotting, the faculties dulled. Or those who have died before their time — a body one day dead, or two days, or seven, devoured by crows and magpies, starving dogs, kites and vultures, foxes, wolves, and jackals, all manner of fierce and savage beasts and birds. Or, once life has ended, the body carried out and placed on a high bier beneath a canopy, the assembled crowd before and behind either grieving in silence or wailing aloud, ashes and dust scattered over the body and hair, giving rise to sorrow, suffering, grief, resentment, distress, and anguish. All such forms as these I should observe. Observing these forms accords with pure conduct, supports pure conduct, and gives rise to wholesome deliberation.

items.title: Entering a Patron's House: Posture, Seating, and Deportment

items.zh: 不應搖身、搖臂、搖頭、跳躑、携手、叉腰、竦肩入施主家，不應輒坐所不許座，不應不審觀座而坐，不應放縱一切身分，不應翹足、不應交足、不太狹足、不太廣足，端嚴而坐。
items.en: One should not enter a patron's house swaying the body, swinging the arms, shaking the head, hopping about, holding hands with another, hands on the hips, or shoulders hunched up. One should not sit in a seat one has not been offered; one should not sit down without first examining the seat carefully; one should not let any part of the body go slack. One should not cross one leg over the other, nor sit with the legs crossed, nor with the feet too close together, nor too far apart — one should sit upright and dignified.

items.title: Wearing the Robe and Handling the Bowl in a Patron's Home

items.zh: 不應開紐、不軒、不磔，亦不褰張而被法服；所服法衣並皆齊整，不高、不下、不如象鼻；非如多羅樹間房穗、非如龍首、非如豆摶而被法服。不應持鉢預就其食，不應持鉢在飲食上，不應置鉢在雜穢處、若坑㵎處、若崖岸處。
items.en: One should not wear the Dharma robe with its fastenings undone, hiked up, torn, or hanging open. The robe worn should be entirely even — neither too high nor too low, not drooping like an elephant's trunk; not uneven like the gaps between palm-tree fronds, not bulging like a dragon's head, not puffed out like a lump of bean paste. One should not hold the bowl and approach the food ahead of time [before it is served, or before the community begins eating]; one should not rest the bowl on top of food or drink; one should not set the bowl down in a filthy place, a ditch, or the edge of a cliff.

items.title: Taking a Meal With Real Care

items.zh: 又應次第受用飲食。不應以飯覆羹臛上，不以羹臛覆其飯上，不應饕餮受諸飲食，不應嫌恨受諸飲食，不太麁食、不太細食，不應圓摶食，不應舐手、不應舐鉢，不振手食、不振足食，不應齧斷而食其食。
items.en: One should also take food in the proper order. One should not cover the soup with rice, nor cover the rice with soup; one should not receive food with gluttonous greed, nor with resentment [at food not to one's liking]; one should not pick out only the coarsest food, nor only the finest; one should not roll food into large balls; one should not lick the hand, nor lick the bowl; one should not shake the hand or the foot while eating; one should not tear food apart with the teeth while eating it.

items.title: Walking Meditation Revisited: Where, When Not To, and How

items.zh: 從施主家還歸住處，於晝夜分，在自別人所經行處往反經行；非於他處、非不委處、非不恣處、非不與處而輒經行。非身劬勞、非身疲倦、非心掉舉所制伏時而習經行。為修善品、為善思惟，內攝諸根、心不外亂而習經行，不太馳速、不太躁動，亦非一向專事往來而習經行，時時進步、時時停住而習經行。
items.en: Having returned from a patron's house to one's dwelling, one paces back and forth, by day and by night, in a walking-meditation space specifically one's own — not in another's space, not in an unfamiliar space, not in a space where one cannot move freely, and not in a space the community has not allotted. One does not practise walking meditation when overcome by bodily exertion, bodily fatigue, or mental restlessness. For the sake of wholesome cultivation and correct reflection, drawing the faculties inward with the mind undistracted, one practices walking meditation neither too fast nor too agitated, and not simply pacing back and forth continuously, but advancing and pausing by turns.

items.zh: 如是於自所居住處、自院自房自別人處、僧分與處、非於他處、非不委處、非不恣處習經行已。
復於大床，或小繩床，或草葉座，或尼師壇，或阿練若、樹下、塚間、或空閑室，結加趺坐，端身正願，安住背念，而習宴坐。於夜中分如法寢息，於晝日分及夜初分，修諸善品不應太急。如是寢時，應如前說，住光明想、正念、正知、思惟起想。於夜後分速疾覺寤。
items.en: …Then, on a large bed, a small rope bed, a grass seat, a sitting-cloth, in a forest dwelling, under a tree, near a charnel ground, or in a quiet room, one sits cross-legged, holds the body upright, forms a correct resolve, and abides turned from unwholesome thought — this is sitting meditation. In the middle watch of the night, one sleeps properly; through the day and the first watch, one cultivates wholesome practices without undue haste. When lying down, one should, as explained before, abide in the perception of light, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and the intention to rise. In the last watch, one wakes swiftly.

items.title: Section: Speech and Silence, First Meaning — Setting Aside Worldly Writing for Genuine Reflection

items.zh: 或於語論、或於讀誦，勤修加行。或為修斷，閑居宴默思惟法時，應當遠離順世典籍，綺字、綺句、綺飾文詞，能引無義，不能令證神通等覺、究竟涅槃。復於如來所說正法，最極甚深、相似甚深空性相應，隨順緣性及諸緣起，殷重無間善攝善受，令堅、令住、令無失壞，為成正行，不為利養恭敬稱譽。又於是法言善通利、慧善觀察，於諠雜眾不樂習近、不樂多業、不樂多言，於時時間安住正念。
items.en: Either in discussion or in recitation, one diligently applies effort. Or, for the sake of cutting off the afflictions, dwelling alone in quiet silence to reflect on the teaching, one should avoid worldly writings, ornate words, ornate phrases, and ornate expressions — these lead only to what is meaningless, and cannot bring about the realisation of higher knowledge, awakening, or final nirvana. One should instead, regarding the true Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata — the utterly profound, and the seemingly profound teaching connected with emptiness, in accordance with conditionality and dependent origination — earnestly and without interruption take it up well and hold it well, making it firm, making it abide, never letting it be lost, so as to accomplish correct practice, not for the sake of gain, honour, or praise. One should further become fluent in the words of this teaching, examine it with wisdom, take no pleasure in mixing with noisy crowds, take no pleasure in excessive activity, take no pleasure in excessive talk, and abide in mindfulness at all times.

items.zh: 與諸有智同梵行者，語言談論，共相慶慰，樂興請問，樂求諸善，無違諍心。言詞稱量、言詞合理、言詞正直、言辭寂靜，樂勤為他宣說正法。又應宴默，於惡不善所有尋思不樂尋思，又於非理所有諸法不樂思惟。

blocks.text: The second pass continues: what one should look at, how to behave as a guest, and walking and sitting again.
Old age, illness, and death: a funeral, with "dust and earth covering the body and hair". Master Cháng Bǎi explains the mourners' custom. These sights turn the mind towards practice.

"One should not sit in a seat not offered; one should not sit without first examining the seat." Master Cháng Bǎi: sit on the front third of the seat, back straight, feet on the floor. Food is taken in order of seniority; one does not prepare one's bowl before the community begins.

Walk in one's own space, not another's, and not when exhausted or restless. Master Cháng Bǎi: "walk a few steps, stop, and see whether the mind has run off and whether the object is still there; then walk on."

"Through the day and first watch, one cultivates the good without undue haste." Master Cháng Bǎi: too much haste overheats you. He quotes the *Avataṃsaka*: "Sitting upright, may all beings sit on the seat of awakening."

"One should avoid worldly writings, ornate words and phrases; they lead only to what is meaningless." One reflects instead on what is truly profound. Venerable Miào Jìng: the utterly profound is the ultimate truth the Buddha realised.

quiz.q: At a funeral, "ashes and dust scattered over the body and hair" — whose body? How do the masters differ?
options: both say on a Buddha image
Cháng Bǎi: on the deceased's body and hair; Miào Jìng: mourners soil their own body and hair
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: much dust and earth gathered, covering the deceased's body and hair. Venerable Miào Jìng: one soils one's own body and hair with ash and dust. The translator's note follows the mourners' reading.

quiz.q: What does the treatise require about sitting in a patron's house, and what example does Master Cháng Bǎi give?
options: sit anywhere; take the biggest seat
not sitting where not invited, not sitting without examining the seat; one might sit on cake or chewing gum
sit on the floor; it's cleaner
quiz.why: "One should not sit in a seat one has not been offered; one should not sit down without first examining the seat carefully." Master Cháng Bǎi: sit without looking, and there may be a piece of cake or chewing gum on it.

quiz.q: What concrete way of sitting "upright and dignified" does Master Cháng Bǎi describe?
options: sit on the front third of the seat, back naturally straight, feet on the floor
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: sit on the front third of the seat; the back straightens naturally, the feet must touch the floor — this is sitting upright and dignified.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain "in the proper order" in "take food in the proper order"?
options: by monastic seniority — the most senior eat first
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: food should be taken in order of monastic seniority; those with more years in the precepts eat first.

quiz.q: After returning from a patron's house, where does the treatise say one should do walking meditation?
options: in one's own walking area — not another's, not unfamiliar, not where one can't move freely, not unallotted
quiz.why: "One paces back and forth … in a walking-meditation space specifically one's own — not in another's space, not in an unfamiliar space, not in a space where one cannot move freely, and not in a space the community has not allotted." Venerable Miào Jìng: one's walking space is one's own, not shared with others.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain "advancing and pausing by turns," and with what practice does he contrast it?
options: walk fast nonstop; compared with tai chi
stand still; compared with standing meditation
walk a few steps, stop, and check whether the mind has wandered and the object remains; Chinese Chan walks fast and stops at the sound of the board
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: walk a few steps, stop, and observe whether the mind has run off and whether the object is still there; look inward, then walk on. In Chinese Chan, by contrast, one walks fast and the board is struck to make everyone stop.

quiz.q: Why should one avoid worldly writings when reflecting on the teaching in solitude?
options: they lead to the meaningless and cannot bring higher knowledge, awakening, or nirvāṇa
quiz.why: "One should avoid worldly writings, ornate words, ornate phrases, and ornate expressions — these lead only to what is meaningless, and cannot bring about the realisation of higher knowledge, awakening, or final nirvana." Venerable Miào Jìng: however beautiful worldly prose is, studying it won't give you higher knowledge.
